📉 Value at Risk (VaR): The Language of Modern Risk Management

Every investment carries risk. But the ability to measure and understand that risk is what enables better decision-making. This is where Value at Risk (VaR) plays a vital role.

Value at Risk (VaR) is a statistical measure that estimates the maximum potential loss a portfolio could experience over a specified time period at a given confidence level.

Example:
If a portfolio has a 1-Day VaR of ₹100,000 at a 95% confidence level, it means that under normal market conditions, there is a 95% probability that the portfolio will not lose more than ₹100,000 in a single day. The remaining 5% of the time, losses could exceed this amount.

Why VaR Matters:
• Measures market risk
• Monitors portfolio risk exposure
• Supports capital allocation decisions
• Forms the foundation for stress testing
• Widely used by banks, asset managers, hedge funds, and regulators

You can't effectively manage what you can't measure. VaR transforms risk into a quantifiable metric, enabling more informed investment and risk management decisions.

One nuance worth adding: VaR is more naturally understood as a quantile of the distribution of a risk variable than as a "maximum potential loss."
 
Three reasons I find that framing useful. It makes the modeling assumptions explicit — the estimate is only as good as the distribution you assume or estimate. It also generalizes beyond P&L: liquidity-adjusted VaR models the distribution of bid-ask spreads and takes an adverse quantile to build the liquidity add-on. And it makes the step to Expected Shortfall and broader tail-risk modeling natural, since ES is just an average over the tail beyond that quantile.

VaR is useful for quantifying risk, but the 95% confidence level shouldn’t be mistaken for a guarantee that losses beyond ₹1 lakh will happen only 5% of the time. The measure is most useful when its assumptions and limitations are understood alongside it.
